Stated Claim / Post Context:
53-year-old doctor salsa dances to keep her brain sharp: Here are a few more of her habits for a long, healthy life

Dr. Suzanne Ferree equips her patients with daily practices for optimal health. Here's how she structures her own routine for longevity.

Actual Article Body:
Related Stories

Dr. Suzanne Ferree is a human performance and longevity expert who sees patients in their mid-40s to mid-60s and equips them with practices for optimal health. Ferree has been studying longevity since 2014.

"Originally, I was seeing a lot of older patients that were already in disease state, and I started to realize I needed to be able to catch them earlier," says Ferree, who is also the founder of Vine Medical Associates in Georgia, where she serves as the senior physician.

She realized the sweet spot for improving health outcomes later in life for older adults is midlife between the ages of 45 and 65.

"That's where I feel like I can make the most impact, and where the patients, if they do [make] some changes, can make the most impact," she says.

At 53 years old, much of what Ferree shares with her patients she incorporates in her own routine. Here's how she structures her life to improve her healthspan.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

CNBC Make It: What are some things that you're doing to keep your body healthy?

One of the things I love is an app called Think Dirty, and it is based on the Environmental Working Group's information about the toxicity of chemicals that we're exposing ourselves to. The Think Dirty app is primarily regarding personal care products like shampoo, soap, hair spray, etc. And so I try to choose the least toxic option.

If you barcode scan your items, like your shampoo for example, it will tell you how toxic that particular item is, what's toxic about it, and give it a score. And then it will give you a link to an alternative option that is less toxic for you.

I've read everybody else talking about sleep, and that's so important, getting quality sleep. But I would say, if I could add a different dimension to it, getting my last meal a couple of hours before sleep allows my body to not be busy digesting, but busy taking care of the clean-up process at night. That really restorative sleep where the immune system, or the sort of trash system of the brain opens up, everybody dumps their trash, and the trash trucks come by and takes it out of the system.

Also, moving my body in significant ways. Anything that's anti-sedentary. So that would be things like walking my dog, taking a yoga or Pilates class. I do a private session with a Pilates instructor, and I do some weight training because I believe that muscle's the currency of aging. I will run occasionally. I try to mix it up, because I feel like routine is not super helpful for me personally. I like to do different things on different days.

What are you doing specifically for your brain health?

For sure, sleep comes in, getting regular sleep. Also, learning new skills. So for example, learning how to salsa dance. I fairly recently took up salsa dancing.

You're using the top part of your body and the bottom part of your body. The upper part of your body is doing something different than the lower part, and then you're also using your brain. So, the brain is being really triggered.

Salsa is probably one of the best exercises because of that. I guess swing dancing would fall into that same category where you're using the body in different directions at the same time and requiring your brain to memorize steps. Just like you need to work out your muscles, it's important to work out the brain in that way too.

And then meditation. Spending time on a daily basis in some form of meditation. Sometimes that is dancing to music in my living room. Sometimes it's actually sitting in a lotus position and using a mantra.

Another thing that I hear about is the importance of connecting with others for longevity, of having those healthy, positive relationships in your life. What's your social fitness like, and how are you getting that social interaction?

I have a significant other, my partner. It's nice to spend time with him and his family and my own family. I have girlfriends that I do things with during the week and on the weekends.

Sex is, of course, important. I think if we're keeping ourselves sexually interested, then that's a sign of a healthy body. And then I have a community that I spend time with. It's out of town, and I go do sort of a yoga meditation retreat with them on a periodic basis.

What are some of the foods that you're getting into your daily diet for optimal health?

I think as many colors as I can possibly get. The order of how you eat your food is important, so eating vegetables first, protein second, and any carbohydrates, including drinks, as your last intake is the way to go.

It helps with slowing down that glucose absorption, so that you're not getting such high spikes of blood sugar.

I try to eat whole foods. So rather than eating things that are packaged or processed, I like to eat things like asparagus and sweet potatoes. One of my favorite sweet potatoes is this purple sweet potato that we get at Sprouts, and it's delicious.

I'm always interested in seeing what longevity experts are reading. So what are you currently reading?

I'm reading a book called "Conscious Loving," and before that, I read a book called "The More Beautiful World Our Hearts Know is Possible." And right now, I'm almost done with "The Midnight Library" for some fiction.

Calming tricks I use on my 7-year-old that work on me, too | CNN

As a parent, I’ve learned some invaluable tips to prevent my kid from having a meltdown. Now, I’m stealing them for myself.

Actual Article Body:
Parenting requires a lot of learning on the job. Raising a 7-year-old, I’ve benefited enormously from the wisdom of teachers, psychologists and other caregivers who have taught me ways to navigate a minefield of tantrums and meltdowns.

The more I learn about how to help a little kid through big feelings, the more I realize I need these strategies as much as my son does.

Adults often get so wrapped up in the demands of everyday life that we don’t recognize when we’re struggling emotionally, Dr. Jessi Gold, chief wellness officer for the University of Tennessee System and associate professor of psychiatry at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences in Memphis, told me. “We are really focused on the task, not the person doing the task.”

Parents teach their kids that their feelings are valid and treat them with compassion, she added, “but we don’t do that to ourselves.”

So I’ve started stealing these parenting tricks for myself — and you don’t need to be a parent to make them work for you.

A time-out is usually used as punishment, but I submit it can also be a gift you give yourself. When I am feeling overwhelmed — usually because my kid is asking more of me than I can deliver in the moment — sometimes the only way to keep from yelling, “Could everyone just shut up?!” is to remove myself from the situation. I send myself to my room.

Being a parent is hard work and ‘massively inconvenient.’ Dr. Becky Kennedy offers 5 tips to help you cope

It’s a “preemptive time-out,” Gold told me. Stepping away from the thing that’s causing the extreme stress or emotion gives you a chance to cool down before saying something you might regret, she said.

When I can’t physically escape, saying something like, “I need a minute,” buys me time to collect myself.

I stole this one from a preschool handout intended to help pint-size pupils manage their outsize reactions. Young kids tend to respond to spilled milk-level challenges with DEFCON 1-level intensity. It wasn’t until recently that I realized I do the same thing.

Maybe I don’t scream and cry and throw myself on the floor, but in my head I’m freaking out. I am inclined to sweat the small stuff, make mountains out of molehills, and let the perfect be the enemy of the good. I will obsess and ruminate and beat myself up for minuscule mistakes. Or spend a disproportionate amount of time and energy weighing a low-stakes decision.

Now I try to channel the wisdom of a preschool teacher and ask myself: Is this a big or little problem? If it’s a little one, I can address it quickly or maybe not, but either way I stop letting it rent so much space in my head and push myself to move on.

It is hard for a kid to switch from one thing to the next, whether it’s ending playtime to have dinner or putting on shoes to go outside. Transitioning from one activity to another commonly triggers tantrums, according to the Child Mind Institute, a mental health nonprofit. One way to forestall that is to offer a preparatory countdown. It can be something like: “Five more minutes of playing, then we’re leaving the park.”

We give kids structured schedules to make their day more predictable and make it clear what’s expected of them. We could give ourselves the same courtesy, Gold said.

What ‘gentle parenting’ does for your kids

I’ve recently learned (with the help of a therapist who specializes in ADHD) that I need a countdown clock of my own. I easily lose track of time, especially when I am focused on something, such as writing this article.

I’ll know, for example, that I need to leave work in an hour. Then I will look up from my screen to find that 75 minutes have passed. Experts call this “time blindness.” Now I give myself a five- to 15-minute warning (in the form of a calendar alert or phone alarm) before I need to wrap up what I’m doing.

It’s so simple and so profoundly helpful. There are several ways that slow, deep breathing can help diffuse stress. It can ratchet down the infamous fight-or-flight response, slow a racing heart, stabilize blood pressure, and stimulate the vagus nerve to trigger the part of your nervous system that makes you feel relaxed.

Whenever my son gets worked up, my go-to move is to tell him to take three deep breaths and count to five. You fell down and skinned your knee? Oh no, let’s take three deep breaths. You’re on the verge of a tantrum because I turned off the TV? Three deep breaths. Nervous walking into a new classroom? I hear you, dude: three deep breaths.

I’ll slowly inhale through my nose and exhale through my mouth to show him what I want him to do. Secretly, I am also trying not to lose it.

Breathe better to live better: Why breathing is your superpower

There is a reason that parents of young children travel with snacks: We know that a hangry kid is a recipe for disaster. Yet I’ll run for hours on a cup of coffee during a busy day, then wonder why I feel unfocused, bedraggled and downright grouchy. It could be burnout or a migraine or the patriarchy — or I might just be dehydrated.

“Our physical health is integrated very much into our mental health,” Gold said. If you don’t eat, drink or sleep, “you’re going to be meaner and crankier, and you’re going to cry when you don’t expect it, just like your kids would.”

It is amazing what a glass of water and a handful of pistachios can do. If only we all had a mom with a purse full of snacks to help us through the day.
